stations.source: Everything starts with HR, the official list of who works here. In the lab a spreadsheet plays HR. When HR adds, moves or removes a person, the accounts follow. Nobody creates an account by hand. Why this way: if access came from anywhere else, HR and IT would drift apart and leavers would keep access.
stations.directory: Two directories kept in step. Active Directory on the Windows server is what the hospital's PCs and older systems check logins against. Entra is the cloud copy every modern app checks. Cloud Sync copies accounts up from the server to the cloud, so fixing a person once fixes them everywhere. Why two: the old on-site directory cannot be switched off while PCs and legacy systems need it, and the cloud one is what modern apps and sign-in rules need.
stations.joiner: What a new hire gets on day one, and how extras are requested. Standard access comes from the job: a nurse gets nurse systems automatically. Anything extra is requested, approved by a manager, and expires. Some combinations are blocked because one person holding both would be a fraud risk. Why: day-one access by job removes the ticket queue, and expiring extras stop access piling up over the years.
stations.apps: The places staff actually go after they sign in. AWS: the cloud console engineers use to run servers. ServiceNow: the help desk where staff raise IT tickets. Okta: a partner clinic's own login system. Each one trusts the hospital login instead of keeping its own passwords, and for AWS the account is created and removed automatically from HR. Why one login: one place to turn a person off, one set of sign-in rules, no forgotten passwords in each app.
stations.signin: The checks at the door, every time someone signs in. Where you are, what device, how risky this looks, and whether you proved it is you with more than a password. New rules start in report-only mode (it watches and logs, blocks nothing) so a mistake cannot lock a nurse out mid-shift. Why watch-only first: a bad rule in a hospital locks out clinicians mid-shift, so rules prove themselves before they enforce.
stations.privileged: Nobody keeps admin power all day. Admins ask for it, say why, get it for a few hours, and it switches off again. Shared passwords for servers live in a vault that rotates them and records who used them. Why: a stolen admin account that holds power all day is the worst case. Power that switches off limits the damage to hours.
stations.detect: The alarm system. Sign-in and change records flow into one place, rules written as code spot trouble such as an admin sign-in from a new country, and a person approves any lockout before it happens. Why a human approves lockouts: an automatic lockout of the wrong clinician is itself a patient-safety incident.
stations.leaver: When someone leaves, HR flips one field and everything closes: account off, sessions cut, app access gone, each step timed. Robot accounts the person owned are handed to someone else so nothing is orphaned. Why timed: the gap between someone leaving and losing access is the number an auditor asks for.
stations.proof: Showing an auditor it works, on demand. Regular reviews of who has what, an evidence binder where every page is fingerprinted and stored where nobody can edit it, and a nightly check that nothing has drifted from the approved setup. Why: a control nobody can prove is a control nobody can trust. Evidence is produced by the system, not assembled by hand before an audit.

SSO: AWS's own login door, set to trust the hospital login. An engineer signs in with her hospital account and has no separate AWS password. SCIM is the part that creates her AWS account when HR hires her and removes it when HR says she left.
A second building that accepts our staff badge.
SNOW: The IT help desk. Staff raise tickets here and IT tracks changes here. It is set to accept the hospital login, so there is no separate ServiceNow password. The free developer copy stands in for the real one.
OKTA: A partner clinic the hospital bought, which already has its own login system. Okta is set to trust Entra, so the clinic's staff keep signing in through their own door but land under the hospital's rules.
The acquired building's reception, now checking our badges.
HR: The spreadsheet that plays the HR system. Every hire, move and exit starts as a row here. A change touching more than ten people is stopped as a safety check.
AGENT: A small program on the Windows server that picks up each HR change and creates or updates the account in Active Directory.
AD: Active Directory: the on-site login system that hospital PCs and older systems check against. Runs on one Windows server here.
The filing cabinet, with a leavers' drawer.
ADCS: The server's certificate service. It issues DC01 a certificate so other systems, like the password vault, can talk to the directory over an encrypted connection.
An ID card for the server.
SYNC: Copies accounts from the on-site directory up to Entra every few minutes. The most powerful admin accounts are kept out of the copy on purpose.
ENTRA: The cloud login system. It holds who you are, which groups you are in, which apps you may open, how you must prove it is you, and who may become an admin.
The front desk and badge office.
CABASE: The core sign-in rules: everyone proves it is them with more than a password, admins must use a phishing-proof method, and old insecure sign-in protocols are blocked.
PIM: Admin rights are something you switch on, not something you own. The most powerful ones need approval and last four hours.
KV: Azure's locked box for the few secrets the automation needs, reachable only from inside the lab network.
A deposit box off a private corridor.
LA: The log store plus the alarm rules. Sign-in and server logs land here, and rules written as code raise an alert on suspicious patterns.
The CCTV archive and the security desk.
LEAVER: HR marks the person as left. A script then disables the account, cuts live sessions and removes app access, timing each step.
Collecting every badge at the exit.
NHI: Robot accounts: the identities apps use to talk to each other. The rule is two human owners each and no stored passwords. The inventory found four without an owner, which is the list being worked.
EVID: One command collects the proof: exports, screenshots and logs, each fingerprinted so tampering would show, filed against the SOX and HIPAA controls they satisfy.
The audit binder, every page fingerprinted.
WORM: Storage where files can be added but never changed or deleted, so evidence cannot be tampered with.
DRIFT: A nightly read-only check: read the live setup, compare it to the approved one in code, and open an issue if anything differs.
A nightly stock-take of every door and lock.
LCW: Automatic first-day and last-day tasks. On day one the manager gets a one-time pass to hand the new hire. On the last day the account is closed out.
A first- and last-day checklist that runs itself.
DYNGRP: Groups that fill themselves. All-Nurses is built from a rule on the HR department, so nobody adds or removes members by hand.
A ward list that rewrites itself.
BIRTH: The standard access a job comes with. Department plus title decides it. No request, no approver, no expiry, because it is the job.
AP: Extras beyond the job. Someone requests, a manager approves, it expires in six months. Guests from a partner tenant come in the same way.
SOD: Combinations one person must never hold, nine pairs in the lab. Refused at request time, or reported if they slip through.
Two bundles nobody may hold together.
INTUNE: Admin portals only open from a managed, healthy laptop. In a pilot here.
A health stamp on the laptop.
CARISK: If Microsoft rates the user as high risk: extra proof and a password change. If the sign-in itself looks risky: blocked.
CAPR: Passkeys instead of passwords, in a pilot. Adding a new sign-in method needs a one-time pass or a phishing-proof method.
A badge only the real door accepts.
CASESS: Admins must sign in again every four hours. The most powerful admins need a step-up. A shared-workstation rule is written but matches no device yet.
A fresh check at the secure wing.
BG: Two emergency Global Admin accounts that sit outside every rule, so a bad rule can always be undone. They are meant to use hardware keys; those are not registered yet, which is tracked. Any use raises an alarm.
HDAU: Help-desk staff can reset standard staff only. Executives and admins sit outside their reach.
VAULT: Finds the most powerful server passwords, rotates them, and hands them out only against an approved change ticket.
A key cabinet that re-keys itself after use.
GUAC: An admin works on a server through a recorded session and never sees the password.
A recorded room you enter without the key.
HA: The vault runs as three copies that agree, with failover and a timed restore drill, so losing one never locks admins out.
DYN: A database login made on request and deleted after one hour.
A key cut for one hour.
CONJUR: Programs fetch only the secret their policy allows, nothing else.
K8S: A container trades a ten-minute token for one secret. Not covered in the walkthrough.
PB: Every alert is pushed to a Teams channel and opened as a ServiceNow ticket automatically.
CONTAIN: A person approves in Teams. Then sessions are cut and the account disabled or flagged.
FEED: Every password check-out from the vault is matched against who actually logged into the server.
SPLUNK: A second alarm system running the very same detection rules, to show they aren't tied to one product. Proven on this machine: every rule fired on a replay of the synthetic test events. The replay of real tenant logs has not run yet.
REVIEW: Managers confirm who still needs what. Riskier access is reviewed more often. Core clinical access is never removed just because nobody answered.
MID: The same review run in a non-Microsoft tool over the mock HR users, each decision recorded as its reviewer.
KPI: Scorecards and security scans taken before and after the build, so improvement is measured, not claimed.
OPMODEL: Who decides what, which meeting happens when, the service levels, and what gets reported to the CISO and the board.
The org chart for decisions, not people.
